claim: Opening: one higher-dimensional object casts different shadows depending on the angle of the light; the Four Pillars are four shadows of one thing, and 'these are all views of the same thing.' § Kaleidoscope, Crystal, and Wallpaper: a kaleidoscope multiplies one fragment through symmetry — 'the viewer isn't seeing more stuff; they're seeing the same fragment from many angles' — and the pillars are 'symmetry operations' on one fundamental domain.

pieces.what: One object, many shadows: a 4D object (a tesseract, or a closed 4D Lissajous trajectory) projected to the plane, with the light's angle under the reader's hand. The test comes last: four shadows are shown and the reader must say whether they could all come from one object or must come from two — chance level and verdict rule stated before the first trial, both arms scored (one-object sets and two-object sets). Tests whether 'one thing, four shadows' is distinguishable from 'four things' at all, which is what the opening claims.
pieces.walks_up_from: a cube's shadow on a wall, at one angle

pieces.what: The Lissajous-in-a-sphere identity rebuilt live: two or three oscillators with frequency-ratio sliders; the trace is a projection of a trajectory on a torus. Tests the section's own claim that 'the pattern changes depending on the frequency relationships' — a rational ratio closes the curve, an irrational one fills the surface — and shows the same figure at the four interpretive levels only if the page's four levels are real readings of one trace, not four captions.

A kaleidoscope: one fragment multiplied through a chosen symmetry group, the group switchable among a few wallpaper groups. Tests 'the viewer isn't seeing more stuff' by counting: the information in the tiling is the fragment's, and the piece shows a tiling can be recovered from its fundamental domain plus the group and nothing else. Then the page's harder claim: can four 'canonical symmetries' be a group? The piece shows the two groups of order four (cyclic and Klein) acting on a domain and lets the reader see what the four projections would be under each — a probe of the open question, not an answer; whatever it finds is an offer.

note: October nomination (the weave asked for it by name); weight here is the cloud pilot's, matching the board's other concept pages. The page says the logo patch is P5.js in one place and 'the Max/MSP patch' in another — the Context says which is true is Loudon's to say: an offer if a piece touches it, never a correction.
